Students will learn the basics of typography, color theory, layout, composition, and data visualization, and practice expressing their ideas by sketching, whiteboarding, and using modern digital design tools. Students will also learn to question the design choices as well as seek and provide effective feedback through design critiques. Other topics may include storyboarding, fundamentals of user interface design, design systems, and physical product prototyping. Students will create a variety of artifacts: concept posters, communication flyers, digital advertisement banners, data visualizations, brand identities, video storyboards, etc. This is a required course in the MIIAS and MIIPS degree programs. All other students must put themselves on the waitlist and contact the instructor for permission.

49745.title: Special Topics in Integrated Innovation
49745.description: Special Topics in Integrated Innovation is an opportunity for students to gain a deeper understanding of a specific area in this field. Sections will vary in topic and change from semester to semester. Fall 2026: Moonshot Thinking and Sustainability The Moonshot Thinking and Sustainability course is about radical innovation toward solving some of the world's wickedest problems. We want to move your thinking beyond design and design engineering into a learning space inspired by X the Moonshot Factory. A space where students from diverse backgrounds can work on interdisciplinary teams to explore "impossible" solutions to achieve 10x improvements across a wide range of topics. If you want to maximize your impact for good and change lives for the better on a grand scale, this is the course for you.

49746.title: Integrated Innovation Institute Internship
49746.description: This course is for students in the MIIPS Advanced Study 16 month program who are pursuing an internship. Internships work can be conducted on-site with a company or thru sponsored projects at the Integrated Innovation Institute. At the end of the summer, students will submit a paper reflecting on their internship experience and how it relates to the MII-PS curriculum. Special permission is required to be enrolled in this course. This course is only offered during the summer.

49747.title: Mindset Intensive
49747.description: The exploratory nature of the Mindset Intensive course encourages MIIAS students to apply learnings from their Carnegie Mellon University classes, experiences, internships, and backgrounds to research, create, and communicate about an innovation-related topic of interest. Students will use critical thinking, mapping, and making throughout the semester as they follow a self-defined process and plan to build a case for their work. Students who are the most successful in this class make continual progress inside and outside of class time. Students may work alone or in pairs and must choose one of the sections listed below as their area of concentration. While there may be overlaps between sections, e.g., an experience driven innovation through technology, the content and learning in the section is guided through the lens of experience, systems thinking, or technology. All sections may require a final showcase presentation and article about the work. Section A: Systems Thinking Driven Innovation Section B: Experience Driven Innovation Section C: Technology Driven Innovation

49748.title: Independent Study
49748.description: This independent study is designed to give students an opportunity to explore pertinent subjects through faculty directed reading or research. Variable hrs. Once you and the faculty have agreed upon the independent study, send the independent study form to the manager of Integrated Innovation Institute for enrollment. Restricted to only MIIPS students.

49749.title: Independent Study
49749.description: This independent study is designed to give students an opportunity to explore pertinent subjects through faculty directed reading or research. Variable hrs. Once you and the faculty have agreed upon the independent study, send the independent study form to the manager of Integrated Innovation Institute for enrollment. Restricted to only MII-PS students.

49750.title: Integrated Thinking for Innovation
49750.description: The challenges our world is facing today signal an unprecedented need for innovators who can analyze wicked problems, communicate system complexities, and work effectively with stakeholders from multiple industries to generate multiple solution pathways. The toughest problems require us to employ a multi-disciplinary approach and to develop a growth mindset to embrace new ways of thinking and working. Innovators need to understand a problem from multiple perspectives and learn how to empathize and work collaboratively with stakeholders. In this studio course, students practice modeling complex system problems, and engage in critical thinking through process retrospectives and peer- and self-critique of work products. Students will learn and practice a toolkit of methods and frameworks (e.g. systems thinking) to guide intelligent problem exploration and framing.

49751.title: Product Management
49751.description: This course covers the role and responsibilities of Product Management (PM). It covers key PM responsibilities (or areas of involvement) such as customer research, problem definition, product ideation, prototyping, positioning, feature design, documentation & deliverables, the product development process, go-to-market, measurement, and growth, particularly in the internet/software sectors. As well this class will introduce concepts and methodologies that will help train the mind of the PM. Guest speakers are also an important component of this class.

49755.title: Problem Discovery & Definition
49755.description: Students identify and describe meaningful business or social problem that can be improved in part by software technologies. Students apply a variety of techniques to elicit and model customer requirements, perform an analysis of competing products, and write a compelling vision for a creative product or service solution. Students create a product description document that captures solution alternatives for the business or social problem they are solving.

49756.title: Product & Business Modeling
49756.description: This course explores the creation of business models for the problems that the students identified and intend to solve. In order for entrepreneurs to be successful, the ability to extract value from an innovation is essential. This course will introduce the business model framework and how to apply it to convert problem definitions and solution alternatives to economic value. Students will be able to interact persuasively with management to "sell" their product vision. Through teams, students will form specific approaches for business models for selected new business concepts and share them in class discussions.

49757.title: Solution Strategy & Marketing
49757.description: This course provides students with an understanding of commercializing a product in the dynamic high-tech industry. Students apply concepts of effective strategy for effective product delivery. This will include understanding the drivers for a strategic roadmap, creating scenarios for alternatives, market and technology analysis and establishing metrics for business success. Students define a strategy and roadmap for delivering a minimum viable product that addresses the business or social problem they intend to improve.

49758.title: The Business of Software
49758.description: Project teams develop a complete business plan for a software product, including revenue and expense models, as well as sales, marketing, and support mechanisms to define the structure of a successful software business. Priority registration for this course will be designated to Master of Science in Software Management students. Note: The R section of this course is specifically reserved for students in the Part-Time Remote Master of Science in Software Management program.

49759.title: Integrated Innovation for Large-Scale Problems
49759.description: Step into an in‑person, studio‑style course where you'll join peers from design, business, and engineering to grapple with society's most tangled wicked problems. Instead of jumping to solutions, you will slow down to map these problems as living systems: who is involved, how power and incentives flow, and how today's decisions shape tomorrow's realities. Across three immersive modules, you will use systems thinking, futures studies, and design‑led methods to explore both present dynamics and long‑term trajectories. You'll engage in debates, stakeholder role‑plays, and co‑design activities that culminate in short experiential "future scenarios" and facilitated workshops with real stakeholders. The emphasis is on deep problem understanding, strategic framing, and collaborative sense‑making, skills that underpin responsible software and product innovation at scale. Seats are limited and enrollment is by application/acceptance, as the course depends on sustained participation, preparation, and a high level of curiosity.

49760.title: Foundations of Software Management
49760.description: Students apply fundamental methods, models, and frameworks to assess real software companies from a variety of perspectives - marketing, strategy, finance, operations - to understand how businesses organize and make decisions. Working individually and in groups, students develop skills for managing teams and employee performance. Students practice personal leadership. Note: enrollment into this course is reserved for incoming Master of Science in Software Management Students.

49761.title: The Future-Ready Leader
49761.description: Leadership is not defined by titles or authority but by the ability to influence, collaborate, and create meaningful impact. In today's fast-paced, technology-driven world, leaders must navigate complex team dynamics, inspire innovation, and foster environments where people can thrive. This course equips students with the essential leadership competencies needed to excel as effective team members, succeed as team leaders, and refine the skills necessary for managerial roles or entrepreneurial ventures. Through experiential learning, case studies, and applied exercises, students will develop practical leadership techniques that directly apply to their current and future professional settings. The course focuses on five critical leadership skills: strategic questioning to enhance decision-making, compelling storytelling to align and inspire teams, process flow optimization to drive innovation, generative dialogue to foster collaboration, and psychological safety to create inclusive, high-performing teams. It culminates in designing a personal leadership development plan to serve the students as a blueprint for continuous improvement. Whether students are leading teams, preparing for management roles, or launching their own ventures, they will leave this course with the confidence and capability to navigate complex team dynamics and drive meaningful outcomes.

49762.title: Special Topics: AI Engineering Fundamentals
49762.description: This course provides a foundational understanding of modern AI systems, with an emphasis on how product teams build, evaluate, and deploy real-world AI capabilities. Students will learn how large language models work (transformers, embeddings, context windows), how to adapt them (RAG, fine-tuning, LoRA), and how to evaluate them. This class is built for students who want understand the concepts of AI engineering AI and the techniques used to build AI-powered products and features.

49767.title: Organizational Behavior for High Tech Knowledge Industry
49767.description: This course is about "organizational behavior" for high tech knowledge workers. Organizations are essentially human institutions. They are created by people, populated by people, managed by people, developed by people and operated by people. Understanding the fundamentals of human behavior is crucial for success. But people need to be grouped together and "organized" in order to make things happen, often under tight time and budgetary constraints. This course will focus on high tech organizational design and team effectivenessin other words, on the "execution" capability of a knowledge enterprise. Specifically, we will discuss how to organize a team, a business unit, or a company (including start-ups) that are operating in dynamic, global high tech ecosystems. The focus is on agility, flexibility, and the capacity to adapt to new business realities or crisis situations. High tech companies need innovative capabilities, entrepreneurial approaches, cross-silo collaboration, and resilient dispositions. A major challenge is to devise collaborative teams & organizational structures capable of making "sudden turns" and accommodating changing realities.

49770.title: Metrics for Technology Products & Services
49770.description: The Metrics for Technology Products & Services course provides an in-depth understanding and practice of applying metrics to plan and track the development of technology products and services and improve them over time by managing their market performance and value delivery. The course utilizes a business lens to understand and leverage metrics to generate questions and provide answers to meet business and customer goals, including delivered value and performance outcomes. Students will be exposed to a set of metrics architectures and their specific applications at different levels of work aggregation, namely team, program, and portfolio. Value stream mapping and analysis will be taught to identify opportunities for delivering value via adoption, cost reductions, and organizational capabilities. Through team-oriented case study assignments, students can select and design metrics systems to address business needs and value generation for product and service development and operations.

49771.title: Process and Project Management
49771.description: Process and Project Management (PPM) focuses on how software products and services are built, delivered, and sustained efficiently and effectively. While prior courses in the MSSM curriculum emphasize choosing the right products to pursue, this course centers on the disciplined execution required to turn those choices into durable value. The course is grounded in the principles articulated in Project to Product, reframing traditional project management as an end-to-end product value stream that spans Discovery, Development, and Operations. Students will examine how value moves through software lifecycle value streams, why it often stalls, and how organizational structures, operating logic, and leadership behaviors shape outcomes. Flow is treated as the backbone of effective product and process management, with attention to how it manifests differently across Discovery, Development, and Operations. Software development and delivery methods such as Agile, Kanban, DevOps, and hybrid delivery models are examined as ways to express value streams under different organizational constraints, rather than as prescriptive solutions. The course also addresses how AI-enabled and AI-native products fundamentally alter delivery dynamics, introducing probabilistic behavior, new risks, and new opportunities for acceleration, including how generative and agentic AI introduce autonomous decision-making loops that reshape value stream boundaries, risk profiles, and flow governance. Throughout the course, students will learn how leaders can intervene to improve flow without breaking coherence across technical, organizational, and human systems.

49772.title: Software Engineering Management
49772.description: In this course, you will learn the software engineering paradigms that are widely adopted in modern software industry. You will be introduced to the Software Development Life Cycles (SDLC) and its supporting process and tools in each stage. Through team based projects, you will gain firsthand experience on best practices in the art of collaboration and software engineering management. In a high-performing team environment, you will be able to build cloud based mobile applications through iterative process of requirements definition, architecture design, implementation, integration, testing, measurement and deployment. If you have already taken 18-652, Foundations in Software Engineering, you are not eligible to register for this course. Note: enrollment into this course is reserved for incoming Master of Science in Software Management Students.

49779.title: Applied AI (Artificial Intelligence)
49779.description: This Applied AI course is designed to equip students with foundational knowledge in AI while exploring its diverse industrial applications and ethical considerations. Students will gain insights into AI's impact across industries such as Manufacturing, Finance, Healthcare, and Retail. Through interactive lectures, real-world case studies, and exclusive discussions with industry leaders, students will deepen their understanding of both the technical and strategic aspects of AI adoption and innovation. Prerequisites of machine learning courses are strongly preferred but not required.

49780.title: Human Computer Interaction & User Experience
49780.description: An introduction to the field of Human Computer Interaction. The user interface and experience of a system, to a large measure, is perceived by the user as 'the system'. Innate human capabilities are discussed to understand how to make appropriate decision in designing user interfaces. Priority registration will be given to students in the Integrated Innovation Institute. Note: The R section of this course is specifically reserved for students in the Part-Time Remote Master of Science in Software Management program.

49781.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
49781.description: The landscape of software products is being redefined by artificial intelligence. This course provides current and future product managers, entrepreneurs, and technology leaders with a comprehensive introduction to traditional and modern machine learning. We trace a path from the foundational algorithms that turn data into predictions to the powerful architectures that drive today's Generative AI and AI Agents. Through hands-on exercises, students will learn to evaluate, design, and responsibly deploy AI capabilities into innovative products. The course project requires students to design and prototype a novel AI-infused product feature. Some class sessions use a Flipped Classroom model, with lectures viewed offline to dedicate class time to hands-on labs, discussions, and project work. Other class sessions will be delivered as lectures.

49782.title: User-Centered Research Methods for Product Innovation
49782.description: Building great products and services begins with having a deep knowledge of the problem you are solving and the people for whom you are designing. From controlled lab studies to field research, a/b testing to participatory design, learn a host of Human-Computer Interaction research methods and analysis techniques to get you the right insights and on the path to crafting innovative ideas.

49784.title: AI-Native Product Management with LLMs and Agents
49784.description: This course equips students with the product strategy, technical fluency, and responsible innovation to design and manage AI-native products built on large language models (LLMs) and agents. Students will learn how to align technical capabilities with business outcomes by translating cutting-edge AI architectures into impactful, scalable product solutions. Through industry collaboration, hands-on prototyping, and real-world case studies, students will gain end-to-end experience in defining AI product requirements, designing human-in-the-loop systems, prompt engineering, RAG pipelines, and integrating generative and agentic intelligence into software ecosystems while learning to evaluate and govern AI products responsibly. The course is ideal for product managers, engineers, designers and entrepreneurs who seek to lead AI-driven initiatives, strengthen cross-functional collaboration, and bring LLM-enabled products from concept to product.

49785.title: Special Topics: Leading Change for AI Business Transformation
49785.description: Digital Transformation (DTX) is among the most critical initiatives that every enterprise is undertaking today. These initiatives are driven by the need to achieve higher levels of process efficiency and significantly enhance the employee and customer experience. At the heart of this transformation are AI, Generative AI, and increasingly, Agentic AI—autonomous software agents that can reason, take action, and collaborate across complex workflows. These capabilities present unique opportunities to redefine how value is delivered, but they also bring significant changes to work processes, decision-making, and leadership experiences. For such technologies to succeed, they must be supported by significant human change for both internal personnel and customers alike. In this course, students will explore both the enabling technologies of digital transformation and the change management methodologies required to adopt them effectively. Special attention will be paid to the leadership challenges presented by Agentic AI, including organizational readiness, trust, workforce adaptation, and ethical risk. The course integrates the ADKAR model of individual change with the C-AQAL framework (Consciousness-Systems-Culture-Behaviors), which maps the systemic, cultural, and behavioral feedback loops that shape transformation success. Assignments will provide students with the opportunity to apply these frameworks to real-world DTX case studies and develop practical strategies for leading human-centered, AI-augmented transformations.

49787.title: Architecture & Programming Principles
49787.description: Software products are increasingly built as distributed, API‑driven systems that must evolve quickly while remaining reliable, secure, and cost‑effective. The responsibility of Software Product Managers and technical leaders now extends well beyond core features into non‑functional aspects such as cloud platform choices, scalability, interoperability, observability, and responsible use of AI. This course makes students technically savvy about the architecture of modern software products so they can influence design decisions before failures surface in production. Students will learn to analyze layered and service‑oriented architectures, design and critique RESTful APIs, reason about quality attributes (for example, scalability, reliability, security, performance), and understand how patterns such as data pipelines, serverless, and AI services fit into an overall system. Rather than focusing on low‑level coding, the course emphasizes architecture models, trade‑off analysis, and collaboration with engineering teams; light implementation work (primarily in Python and JavaScript) is used to illuminate core concepts. The course also teaches students how to leverage AI‑assisted tools as "junior architects" and code assistants—using them to generate options and tests, while retaining human judgment over system design. Some class sessions use a Flipped Classroom model, where lectures are delivered as short videos and class time is dedicated to clarification, discussion, and working on architecture and API design assignments.

49790.title: Software Management Independent Study
49790.description: Working with the faculty, realize that the faculty are most interested in Independent Study projects that further their own research goals. You may not be successful on your first inquiry, so please be patient. We want you to have a good Independent Study experience, so faculty are encouraged to say "no" if they don't have the cycles to mentor a project. Once you and the faculty have agreed upon the independent study, send the independent study form to the director of your program. Students must submit a proposal and be accepted into the course before being able to register.

49791.title: Software Management Capstone Project
49791.description: Student teams continue work on their product or business idea. Student teams may refine or rework ideas, or continue to extend the work started in previous semesters. A plan, including milestones and deliverables, which is developed by the team must be submitted to and approved by the faculty advisor at the start of this course. Students must submit a proposal and be accepted into the course being being able to enroll.

49796.title: Software Management Independent Study
49796.description: This independent study is designed to give students an opportunity to explore pertinent subjects through faculty directed reading or research. Variable hrs. Once you and the faculty have agreed upon the independent study, send the independent study form to the manager of Integrated Innovation Institute for enrollment. Restricted to only MSSM students. This course is for students who wish to take independent study as a mini instead of full-semester course (49790). Students must submit a proposal and be accepted into the course before being able to register.

49797.title: Special Topics: Advanced AI for Industry & Society
49797.description: This course offers hands-on project-based learning through partnerships with the leading industry player. Students will get opportunities to be trained and shadowed, develop and implement the most innovative AI, cloud and transformative technologies in response to current industry needs. The curriculum is designed to enhance students' industry readiness through practical, impactful projects addressing real- world challenges.

49800.title: Start Up Creation in Practice
49800.description: For MSSM students with the goal of creating a new start up as they are enrolled in the MSSM degree, they have the option of taking this course in the practice of creating a new venture (12 units per semester). Similar to an independent study, but focused specifically on new venture creation, students will work on developing their technology-focused idea into a potentially viable company through this course. Students can work individually or through a team with other MSSM students. Each student (team) must have an approved faculty advisor. Students must submit a proposal and be approved before being accepted into the course.

49801.title: Venture Governance: Founder Decision-Making, Fundraising and Boards
49801.description: This course helps students to structure and build a successful new venture with hands-on role-play as start-up stakeholders and supporting lectures. This course is designed for aspiring founders, CEOs, investors, and key employees of high-tech startup ventures. Learn the essential skills and processes required to lead a startup, avoid pitfalls in co-founder relationships, pursue successful fundraising efforts including pitches, and effectively manage stakeholders such as investors, board members, shareholders, advisory boards, and key employees who invest time and money into your venture. Note: Priority registration is available for the in-person A4 section. The R4 section is reserved for students in the Part-Time Remote MSSM program, with waitlist admissions based on availability.

49803.title: Legal Issues in New Venture Creation
49803.description: A critical part of creating a new venture is to provide the legal structure for both compliance and to prepare the venture for future success. For startups the legal profile of the company sets up the framework for growth. The course will cover basic legal requirements of incorporation, and additional options that need to be determined by the founders including equity distribution, board structure, employee stock option vesting, triggers for contingencies such as firing or acquisition and other issues. Another critical legal issue for both startups and established enterprises surrounds protecting intellectual property to immunize the companys strategic advantage as it gains velocity in the global market and encounters competition. Students will learn about various Intellectual Property tools and strategies to protect their product innovations and to understand the competitive marketplace, both in the US and globally. Priority registration will be given to students in the Master of Science in Software Management program.

51051.title: Study Abroad
51051.description: Students submit a proposal to the faculty study abroad committee. Study abroad can only be for one semester in the junior year, or during any summer.

51101.title: Studio: Survey of Design
51101.description: Students will conduct activities that will help them notice design in the world, investigate how it works, and describe their thinking about design, through photography, video capture, sketching, note-taking and modeling. They will work through projects in various ways as a means of 'testing-out' and reflecting on command design approaches. This course is for undergraduate design majors only.

51102.title: Design Lab
51102.description: Introduce concepts and methods to familiarize students with a range of analog and digital modes of working across products, communications, and environments. Students will use desktop modeling and comping methods to familiarize them with a range of basic materials to build confidence in using and manipulating material to represent ideas. This course is for freshman Design majors only.

51121.title: Visualizing
51121.description: This course introduces basic drawing and sketching techniques including figure-ground translation, 2 pt perspective construction, storyboarding for explanation, diagramming for clarification, field notation for recording through guided exercises, demonstrations, and short projects.

51122.title: Collaborative Visualizing
51122.description: This course introduces frameworks of notational, exploratory and explanatory sketching using collaborative methods and exercises to cooperatively communicate design ideas. This course is for undergraduate design majors only.

51132.title: Introduction to Photo Design
51132.description: Using a digital camera, students learn how to extend their 'seeing' with the camera, both in the world and in a shooting studio. Through shooting assignments student will understand how to: deconstruct image meaning and aesthetical choices, construction of photographic meaning and aesthetics, an understanding of color and how color delivers meaning, how a photographic studio works, proper digital photographic workflow and contemporary trends in photography. Intended for Design Majors, or permission of the instructor.

51150.title: Personal Design Futures
51150.description: It is difficult to go on a lifelong journey without a plan or map. In the "Personal Design Futures" mini-course (PDF), students take on the most important design project: their own life. Students explore who they are, where they come from, and where they hope to go throughout their life. They describe their core values, what makes their life meaningful, and who they wish to become in the future. While one's life is very personal, we use time-tested design methods to explore each person's future. By the end of the mini-course each student will have made a plan for their future. They will be able to explain what matters to them and have charted a way forward. Most importantly, they will know how to rechart their life plans as unexpected events require them to adapt their plans.

51173.title: Human Experience in Design
51173.description: Design touches, and can profoundly affect, people's lives. But why? And how? This course begins with a broad definition of what design is (and can be). We'll see how design is about the process as much as it is about the final product. We'll look at how the end user interacts with what is designed. And we'll discuss how designers need to think beyond the actual artifact to what lies behind it. We'll touch on design theory, design practice, design responsibility and even some design history. And through a series of guest lectures, explorations of other designers' work, field trips, viewings, class discussions and projects, we'll try to determine just what design is and what designers do.

51175.title: Design Studies: Place
51175.description: "Place" introduces you to place-based design thinking. It trains your senses to perceive all that is designed and sustains everyday human lifestyles, especially those infrastructures and services invisible to city dwellers in the built environment. In addition, you will recognize relations between natural and artificial worlds. Coursework covers methods to evaluate individual and collective environmental and social impact at a regional and local level through techniques that develop capacities to reveal dynamic relationships among elements.

51176.title: Design Studies: Futures
51176.description: "Futures" frames design in a temporally-extended, systemic context. It offers essential perspectives, practices, and competencies that are increasingly called for as designers progress in their work and careers, and as the design field evolves to acknowledge its significant powers and responsibilities. You will explore numerous futures methods, which support designers through ideation and storytelling, problem-finding and framing, brief formulation, project coordination, and collaboration. Coursework includes engagement with readings and videos, hands-on creative workshops, and visual prototyping and sketching.

51177.title: Design Studies: Histories
51177.description: Histories explores a plurality of design histories extending beyond the dominant, Anglo-European story of Design. Through a series of guest lectures, critical readings, and offsite explorations, you will expand your understanding of histories, which evolve and change over time in the context of broader social, technological, environmental, economic, and political developments. Coursework includes exploring, developing, and documenting diverse historical perspectives of a research interest of your choice. Final projects will culminate in a presentation of student work.

51178.title: Design Studies: Experience
51178.description: Experience explores how design touches peoples lives, and shapes their materials and non-material worlds. Through a series of lectures, viewings, and class discussions, we'll try to determine just what design is and what designers can do. We will explore contrasting definitions of design, and get to know it as an experientially-rich process. Well examine how users and audiences interact with what is designed, and debate the designers responsibility to consider what lies behind it. Coursework includes individual and team projects exploring design's role in shaping our experience of the world.

51201.title: Communications Studio I: Understanding Form & Context
51201.description: Giving form to messages and information using type, color, and images will be the focus of this introductory studio in Communication Design. Understanding the connection between content, intent, and form will be the goal of every project and exercise. Principles of hierarchy, chunking, sequence, clarity, and visual voice will guide work for the screen and the printed page, in dynamic and static forms.

51203.title: Prototyping Lab I: Communications
51203.description: Learn the core methods and tools of visual communication design, with a focus on Adobe CC: particularly InDesign, Illustrator, Photoshop, Prototyping tools, and After Effects. The learning of software ideally will align with the activities conducted in the Communications Studio. This is a requirement for Design sophomores studying Communications.

51209.title: The Business of Design
51209.description: This course addresses a critical but often missing component of design education: preparing designers for the real-world business dynamics that shape successful careers after graduation. For students who are serious about building meaningful, sustainable careers—or one day leading their own studios—understanding how design operates within the realities of clients, budgets, expectations, market cycles, macroeconomic forces, and relationships is essential. The course also examines why some designers and studios build lasting success while others struggle to sustain momentum, translating industry lessons into practical guidance for young professionals. At its core, design is a business of relationships. This course focuses on client development and management, aligning and exceeding expectations, pricing and value creation, negotiation, communication, and professional positioning. Students explore how trust, perception, and experience shape opportunity—how the client’s perception of the work and the collaboration ultimately defines success. Emphasis is placed on the reality that designers work in service of client goals and outcomes, not in isolation of personal taste. Beyond craft, the course prepares students to think like creative leaders and future founders—learning to work on a business, not just in it. Through real-world case studies, scenarios, and practical examples drawn from professional practice, students gain knowledge rarely taught in design school but essential to building a resilient and rewarding career that can adapt to market cycles, economic shifts, and the evolving realities of the design industry.

51211.title: Products Studio I: Understanding Form & Context
51211.description: This course takes students through a progression of exercises and projects that investigate how object forms can relate to people through reasons of looks, feel, function, make, and preference. The understanding of context plays a role as the system of internal and external factors and conditions that cause people to interact a particular way through how they recognize, handle, move, and perform activity with the form and material of an object. Drawing and physical modeling become essential tools for the planning, development, and communication of these ideas.

51219.title: The Photo Essay
51219.description: Whether traveling for fun or service-learning, be it a short distance to downtown or a flight to a new land, students will learn how to tell a story about place. They will work to make a cohesive narrative and photo essay around location. The photo-essay, in all its varied levels of polish, is often a mainstay of daily life. Photo-essays appear in printed magazines, newspapers, blogs, Instagram feeds, books, catalogs, and even in the context of explaining research in academia. Though the basic structure and components of photo-essay date back as early as 1936 issues of Life Magazine, the style and look of photography has changed over time. Students will learn the historic methodology around creating rich, complex story around place; how images work together to inform one another; and how contemporary images build beauty, poetics and metaphor.
